TO: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Department of Health and Human Services
FILE CODE: CMS-0062-P
FEDERAL REGISTER CITATION: 91 FR 19890 (April 14, 2026)
DATE: April 22, 2026
FROM: Helsesoft LLC / GreenLight PA, Bellevue, Washington
RE: Comment on the 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P)
I. Introduction and Commenter Identity
Helsesoft LLC is a Washington State health technology company and the developer of 
GreenLight PA, a prior authorization intelligence platform built specifically for dermatology. 
GreenLight PA maintains a structured, machine-readable library of prior authorization (PA) 
criteria for dermatology biologics — including agents such as dupilumab, tralokinumab, 
risankizumab, and secukinumab — mapped at the drug, insurer, and state level across major 
commercial payers including Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid managed care plans, 
and commercial QHP issuers. The platform is EHR-independent and contains no protected 
health information (PHI) by architectural design, enabling deployment across practice settings of 
all sizes.
Helsesoft LLC was founded by a physician with direct experience in healthcare workflow design 
and clinical operations, and has built GreenLight PA in close collaboration with practicing 
dermatologists. The company's development work has required sustained, direct engagement 
with payer coverage policy documents across multiple drug-indication combinations, insurers, 
and states — giving us ground-level technical understanding of how prior authorization criteria 
are published, structured, updated, and applied in practice. This comment reflects that 
operational experience.
We strongly support CMS's proposal to extend prior authorization interoperability requirements 
to drugs. The sections below address specific provisions of the proposed rule and respond to 
two of CMS's explicit Requests for Information.
II. Support for Extending Electronic PA Requirements to Drugs
Relevant sections: II.B (Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs); II.C (Improving 
Communications and Decision Timeframes); 91 FR 19890
The 2024 Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule (CMS-0057-F) made meaningful 
progress on non-drug PA but created an anomalous gap for specialties like dermatology where 
virtually all high-cost, high-efficacy treatments are biologics dispensed under pharmacy or 
medical benefits. For a dermatology practice, the practical effect of CMS-0057-F was limited: 
the most burdensome authorization workflows — for drugs like dupilumab, which routinely 
requires multi-step documentation of prior treatment failure across multiple insurers — remained 
entirely outside its scope.
CMS-0062-P closes that gap. We specifically support the following proposed provisions:
•
Section II.B.3: Incorporating drugs covered under a medical benefit into the Prior 
Authorization API for all impacted payers. Biologics for dermatologic conditions are 
frequently billed under the medical benefit (Part B for Medicare Advantage), making this 
provision essential for dermatology.
•
Section II.B.5: Requiring support for the NCPDP Formulary and Benefit Standard, which 
will enable providers and their health IT tools to query formulary information and real-
time coverage status for covered drugs.
•
Section II.C.2: Requiring a specific reason for denial in response to PA requests for all 
drugs. In our experience maintaining payer policy documentation for dermatology 
biologics, denial reasons as currently communicated are frequently generic and 
insufficient to guide resubmission.
•
Section II.C.3: Proposed shorter decision timeframes aligned across MA, Medicaid, 
CHIP, and QHP programs. Standardizing timeframes across program types significantly 
reduces administrative complexity for practices managing patients across payer types.
•
Section II.C.7: Requiring public reporting of PA metrics for drugs. This is the 
transparency foundation on which downstream accountability mechanisms can be built.
III. A Critical Gap: Published Criteria vs. Real-World Approval Behavior
Relevant sections: II.C.7 (Public Reporting of Drug PA Metrics); III.D (Request for Information: 
Step Therapy); 91 FR 19890
We write to draw CMS's attention to a structural problem in the prior authorization ecosystem 
that the proposed rule's transparency provisions begin to address but do not fully reach: the 
divergence between payers' published prior authorization criteria and the criteria actually 
applied in approval and denial decisions.
In maintaining GreenLight PA's structured policy library — which monitors coverage policy 
documents for dermatology biologics across more than 200 drug-insurer-state combinations — 
we have observed systematic patterns in which published payer criteria do not reliably predict 
actual approval behavior. These patterns include:
•
Step therapy sequences documented in published coverage policies that are 
inconsistently enforced in practice, with some insurers approving requests that bypass 
stated requirements while denying others that appear to satisfy them.
•
Documentation standards described in policy language that differ materially from what is 
actually required for approval as reflected in denial rationale communications.
•
Coverage criteria that are updated in practice — through apparent internal guidance — 
without corresponding updates to published policy documents, creating a lag during 
which providers and their tools are operating on outdated information.
These patterns create measurable harm. Providers build PA submissions around published 
criteria that may not reflect what the insurer actually requires, leading to avoidable denials, 
resubmission cycles, and delays in patient access to therapy. The public reporting requirements 
in Section II.C.7 represent important progress, but aggregate approval and denial rate metrics 
do not directly surface whether payers are applying their own stated criteria consistently.
IV. Specific Recommendations
A. Require Drug-Level and Specialty-Level Granularity in Public PA Metrics
Relevant section: II.C.7 (Proposed Requirement To Publicly Report Prior Authorization Metrics 
for Drugs); 91 FR 19890
We recommend that CMS require impacted payers to report PA approval and denial metrics 
disaggregated by therapeutic area or clinical specialty (e.g., dermatology, rheumatology, 
oncology) in addition to the proposed drug-level reporting. Dermatology biologics carry 
authorization burden profiles substantially different from other drug categories: they are typically 
chronic therapies, require documentation of prior treatment failure, and involve step therapy 
sequences that vary significantly by insurer and state. Aggregate drug-level metrics will obscure 
this variation.
Specialty-level disaggregation would enable CMS, researchers, provider organizations, and the 
public to identify areas of disproportionate burden and target oversight accordingly. It would also 
allow specialty societies to monitor payer performance within their domain — a form of 
distributed accountability that requires no additional CMS enforcement infrastructure.
B. Require Payers to Publish Machine-Readable, Structured PA Criteria for Covered 
Drugs
Relevant sections: II.A.4(a)(6) (Da Vinci CRD, DTR, and PAS Implementation Guides); II.B.3 
(Prior Authorization API for Drugs Under Medical Benefit); 91 FR 19890
CMS-0062-P requires payers to implement electronic PA APIs enabling providers to submit 
requests and receive decisions electronically. We strongly support this. However, the ability to 
submit a PA request electronically does not, by itself, ensure that providers understand what the 
payer requires for approval. The underlying PA criteria — step therapy requirements, diagnostic 
thresholds, prior treatment history requirements, quantity limits, and documentation standards 
— remain largely inaccessible in structured, machine-readable form.
The Da Vinci Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD) and Documentation Templates and 
Rules (DTR) implementation guides identified in Section II.A.4(a)(6) represent the right technical 
direction: they are designed to surface coverage requirements to providers at the point of care. 
We recommend that CMS strengthen the proposed rule by requiring impacted payers to 
implement CRD and DTR as mandatory — not merely recommended — components of the 
Prior Authorization API for drugs. This would:
•
Enable providers and health IT tools to surface accurate, payer-specific requirements at 
the point of care, reducing avoidable denials driven by documentation gaps.
•
Create an auditable, structured record of the criteria payers have committed to applying, 
against which actual decisions can be evaluated.
•
Reduce duplicative manual research burden on practices that currently must interpret 
narrative PDF policy documents across multiple payers to determine what is required for 
a given drug.
We acknowledge that payers may seek to protect commercially sensitive aspects of their 
coverage criteria. We do not propose disclosure of proprietary adjudication logic or internal risk 
models. We propose only that the criteria a treating provider must satisfy to obtain approval be 
made available in structured, queryable form via the APIs CMS is already requiring payers to 
build.
C. Response to RFI III.D: Step Therapy
Relevant section: III.D (Request for Information: Step Therapy); 91 FR 19890
CMS's request for information on step therapy (Section III.D) directly implicates the divergence 
problem described in Section III of this comment. Step therapy is the single most consequential 
structural feature of drug PA criteria for dermatology biologics, and it is also the area where the 
gap between published criteria and applied criteria is most pronounced and most harmful.
In our operational experience monitoring payer policy documentation for dermatology biologics, 
step therapy requirements are the most frequently updated, most inconsistently enforced, and 
most difficult to interpret elements of published coverage criteria. We offer the following 
observations in response to CMS's request:
•
Step therapy requirements vary materially across payers and states for the same 
drug. A provider prescribing dupilumab for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis may 
face step therapy requirements ranging from one prior topical agent to multiple systemic 
agents depending on the insurer and the patient's state. Published criteria for the same 
drug can require meaningfully different prior treatment histories across payers, creating 
significant administrative burden for practices managing diverse patient populations.
•
Published step therapy criteria are frequently inconsistent with actual approval 
behavior. We have observed patterns where payers appear to approve requests that do 
not satisfy stated step therapy sequences, and deny requests that do — suggesting that 
internal adjudication guidance diverges from published coverage policy. This divergence 
is opaque to providers and impossible to anticipate from published documents alone.
•
The proposed metrics reporting requirements do not capture step therapy 
compliance. Aggregate approval and denial rates do not reveal whether denials are 
based on the step therapy requirements documented in published policy, unstated 
internal criteria, or administrative deficiencies in submission. CMS should consider 
requiring payers to report denial reasons at a level of granularity that includes the 
specific criterion cited — including whether step therapy requirements were the basis for 
denial.
We recommend that CMS use the step therapy RFI to explore requiring payers to: (1) publish 
step therapy requirements for covered drugs in structured, machine-readable form; (2) include 
step therapy criterion citation in denial reason communications; and (3) attest annually that 
published step therapy requirements reflect criteria actually applied during the reporting period. 
These measures would address the root cause of much of the PA burden that this proposed 
rule aims to reduce.
D. Response to RFI III.C: Improving Implementation of Payer API Technology
Relevant section: III.C (Request for Information: Improving Implementation of Payer API 
Technology); 91 FR 19890
CMS's request for information on improving payer API implementation (Section III.C) raises 
questions directly relevant to our experience as a health IT developer serving specialty 
practices. We offer the following observations:
•
EHR-independent middleware tools are essential for broad provider adoption. The 
electronic PA API framework proposed in CMS-0062-P is designed to enable exchange 
between payers and providers or their EHR systems. In practice, many specialty 
practices — particularly independent dermatology practices, which represent a 
substantial share of the prescribers of dermatology biologics — operate with EHR 
systems that have limited or delayed PA API integration. EHR-independent health IT 
tools that can consume payer APIs and surface PA requirements at the point of care are 
a critical link in the adoption chain. CMS's implementation guidance should explicitly 
acknowledge and support this model.
•
API standardization does not eliminate the need for policy intelligence tools. Even 
with standardized FHIR APIs in place, providers will need tools to interpret coverage 
requirements, compare drug options across payers, and guide PA submission content. 
The intelligence layer — translating structured payer data into actionable clinical 
guidance — remains a product and workflow challenge that the API framework alone 
does not resolve. CMS should consider this when evaluating whether the proposed 
technical requirements are sufficient to achieve the rule's burden-reduction goals.
•
API endpoint publication (Section II.E) will meaningfully improve the developer 
ecosystem. The proposed requirement for payers to report and CMS to publish API 
endpoint information (Section II.E) is a practical improvement that will reduce the 
discovery burden for health IT developers building tools that consume payer APIs. We 
support this provision and recommend that CMS require endpoint publication to include 
API version information and conformance testing results to enable developers to assess 
compatibility without direct payer engagement.
V. Conclusion
Helsesoft LLC and GreenLight PA strongly support CMS-0062-P's extension of electronic prior 
authorization and transparency requirements to drugs. The proposed rule addresses a genuine 
gap in the regulatory framework established by CMS-0057-F and has the potential to 
meaningfully reduce PA burden for patients awaiting access to dermatology biologics and other 
specialty medications.
We urge CMS to strengthen the rule by: making the CRD and DTR implementation guides 
mandatory for drug PA; requiring specialty-level granularity in public metrics reporting; and 
using the step therapy and API implementation RFIs to develop requirements that address the 
divergence between published PA criteria and real-world approval behavior. These additions 
would substantially enhance the rule's impact and create lasting accountability in the drug PA 
ecosystem.
Helsesoft LLC welcomes the opportunity to provide additional technical input to CMS on any of 
the issues raised in this comment. We are available for follow-up at the contact information 
below.
Submitted by:
Helsesoft LLC / GreenLight PA
Seattle, Washington 98105
www.greenlightpa.com

analysis:
**1. COMMENTER INFORMATION**
- Author/Organization name: Helsesoft LLC / GreenLight PA
- Stakeholder type: Technology Vendor
- Credentials or expertise mentioned: Washington State health technology company; developer of GreenLight PA, a prior authorization intelligence platform for dermatology; maintains structured, machine-readable library of PA criteria for dermatology biologics (dupilumab, tralokinumab, risankizumab, secukinumab) mapped across 200+ drug-insurer-state combinations; EHR-independent platform; founded by physician with healthcare workflow design experience; built in collaboration with practicing dermatologists

**2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**
Helsesoft LLC strongly supports CMS-0062-P's extension of electronic prior authorization requirements to drugs, which addresses a critical gap for dermatology where most high-cost treatments are biologics. The company urges CMS to make Da Vinci CRD and DTR implementation guides mandatory (not optional), require specialty-level granularity in public PA metrics, and address the systemic divergence between payers' published PA criteria and their actual approval behavior—a problem causing avoidable denials, resubmission cycles, and patient access delays.

**3. REGULATORY CONTEXT**
- Specific sections/provisions addressed: CMS-0062-P (2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule); builds on CMS-0057-F (2024 Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule); Section II.B (Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs); Section II.C (Improving Communications and Decision Timeframes); Section II.C.7 (Public Reporting); Section III.D (RFI: Step Therapy); Section III.C (RFI: Improving Payer API Implementation); Section II.E (API Endpoint Publication)
- Regulatory citations mentioned: 91 FR 19890 (April 14, 2026); Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, QHP programs
- Standards referenced: FHIR, NCPDP Formulary and Benefit Standard, Da Vinci Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD), Da Vinci Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR), Da Vinci Prior Authorization Support (PAS)

**4. DETAILED POSITIONS**

Topic: Extending Electronic PA Requirements to Drugs
- Position: Strongly Support
- Rationale: CMS-0057-F created anomalous gap for specialties like dermatology where virtually all high-cost, high-efficacy treatments are biologics; most burdensome authorization workflows (e.g., dupilumab requiring multi-step documentation) remained outside scope
- Specific request: Finalize proposed extension to drugs

Topic: Drugs Under Medical Benefit in Prior Authorization API (Section II.B.3)
- Position: Support
- Rationale: Dermatology biologics frequently billed under medical benefit (Part B for Medicare Advantage); essential for dermatology
- Specific request: Incorporate drugs covered under medical benefit into PA API for all impacted payers

Topic: NCPDP Formulary and Benefit Standard (Section II.B.5)
- Position: Support
- Rationale: Will enable providers and health IT tools to query formulary information and real-time coverage status for covered drugs
- Specific request: Require support for NCPDP Formulary and Benefit Standard

Topic: Specific Denial Reasons (Section II.C.2)
- Position: Support
- Rationale: Denial reasons currently communicated are frequently generic and insufficient to guide resubmission based on experience maintaining payer policy documentation
- Specific request: Require specific reason for denial in response to PA requests for all drugs

Topic: Shorter Decision Timeframes Across Programs (Section II.C.3)
- Position: Support
- Rationale: Standardizing timeframes across MA, Medicaid, CHIP, QHP significantly reduces administrative complexity for practices managing patients across payer types
- Specific request: Finalize proposed shorter decision timeframes aligned across programs

Topic: Public Reporting of PA Metrics (Section II.C.7)
- Position: Support with Enhancement
- Rationale: Transparency foundation for downstream accountability mechanisms; but aggregate metrics don't surface whether payers apply their own criteria consistently
- Specific request: Require drug-level AND specialty-level granularity (dermatology, rheumatology, oncology) in public PA metrics; enable identification of disproportionate burden areas; allow specialty societies to monitor payer performance

Topic: Da Vinci CRD and DTR as Mandatory Requirements (Section II.A.4(a)(6))
- Position: Modify/Strengthen (Make Mandatory)
- Rationale: Electronic PA submission alone doesn't ensure providers understand payer approval requirements; underlying PA criteria remain largely inaccessible in structured, machine-readable form; CRD and DTR designed to surface coverage requirements at point of care
- Specific request: Require impacted payers to implement CRD and DTR as mandatory (not merely recommended) components of Prior Authorization API for drugs; enables accurate payer-specific requirements at point of care; creates auditable structured record; reduces manual PDF interpretation burden

Topic: Step Therapy Requirements (RFI III.D)
- Position: Add Structured Requirements
- Rationale: Step therapy is most consequential structural feature of drug PA criteria for dermatology biologics; area where gap between published and applied criteria is most pronounced and harmful; most frequently updated, inconsistently enforced, most difficult to interpret; varies materially across payers/states for same drug; published criteria frequently inconsistent with actual approval behavior; metrics don't capture step therapy compliance
- Specific request: (1) Require payers to publish step therapy requirements in structured, machine-readable form; (2) Include step therapy criterion citation in denial reason communications; (3) Require annual attestation that published step therapy requirements reflect criteria actually applied

Topic: Payer API Implementation (RFI III.C)
- Position: Support with Recommendations
- Rationale: Many specialty practices (especially independent dermatology) operate with EHRs having limited/delayed PA API integration; EHR-independent middleware tools critical for adoption; API standardization doesn't eliminate need for policy intelligence tools to interpret coverage requirements
- Specific request: Implementation guidance should explicitly acknowledge and support EHR-independent health IT tools model; recognize need for intelligence layer translating payer data into clinical guidance

Topic: API Endpoint Publication (Section II.E)
- Position: Support with Enhancement
- Rationale: Practical improvement reducing discovery burden for health IT developers
- Specific request: Require endpoint publication to include API version information and conformance testing results for compatibility assessment

**5. RECOMMENDATIONS**
1. Make Da Vinci CRD and DTR implementation guides mandatory (not optional) components of Prior Authorization API for drugs
2. Require specialty-level granularity (dermatology, rheumatology, oncology) in public PA metrics reporting in addition to drug-level reporting
3. Require payers to publish step therapy requirements for covered drugs in structured, machine-readable form
4. Include step therapy criterion citation in denial reason communications
5. Require payers to attest annually that published step therapy requirements reflect criteria actually applied during reporting period
6. Require API endpoint publication to include API version information and conformance testing results
7. Explicitly acknowledge and support EHR-independent middleware tools in implementation guidance
8. Address divergence between published PA criteria and real-world approval behavior through transparency and accountability measures

**6. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS**

Primary Concerns:
- Systemic divergence between payers' published prior authorization criteria and criteria actually applied in approval/denial decisions
- Step therapy sequences documented in published policies inconsistently enforced; insurers approve requests bypassing stated requirements while denying others that satisfy them
- Documentation standards in policy language differ materially from what's actually required for approval
- Coverage criteria updated in practice through internal guidance without corresponding updates to published policy documents
- Lag period where providers/tools operate on outdated information
- Published payer criteria don't reliably predict actual approval behavior across 200+ drug-insurer-state combinations
- Aggregate approval/denial rate metrics don't surface whether payers apply their own stated criteria consistently
- Aggregate drug-level metrics will obscure variation in burden profiles across specialties
- Electronic PA submission capability alone doesn't ensure providers understand payer approval requirements
- Underlying PA criteria (step therapy, diagnostic thresholds, prior treatment history, quantity limits, documentation standards) remain inaccessible in structured, machine-readable form
- Practices must manually interpret narrative PDF policy documents across multiple payers

Potential Negative Impacts:
- Providers build PA submissions around published criteria that may not reflect actual insurer requirements
- Avoidable denials driven by documentation gaps and criteria mismatches
- Resubmission cycles and delays in patient access to therapy
- Measurable harm from criteria divergence
- Administrative burden from step therapy variations across payers/states for same drug (e.g., dupilumab requirements ranging from one prior topical agent to multiple systemic agents)
- Aggregate metrics reporting doesn't reveal whether denials based on published policy, unstated internal criteria, or administrative submission deficiencies
- Divergence between published and applied criteria opaque to providers and impossible to anticipate

Implementation Barriers:
- Many specialty practices (especially independent dermatology) operate with EHR systems having limited or delayed PA API integration
- API standardization alone doesn't eliminate need for policy intelligence tools to interpret coverage requirements and guide PA submission content
- Intelligence layer challenge translating structured payer data into actionable clinical guidance
- Payers may seek to protect commercially sensitive aspects of coverage criteria

**7. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE**

Data/Statistics Cited:
- GreenLight PA monitors coverage policy documents for dermatology biologics across more than 200 drug-insurer-state combinations
- Systematic patterns observed where published payer criteria don't reliably predict actual approval behavior
- Step therapy requirements for dupilumab can range from one prior topical agent to multiple systemic agents depending on insurer and patient state

Studies/Research Referenced:
- None formally cited; evidence based on operational experience maintaining structured PA policy library

Examples Provided:
- Dermatology biologics: dupilumab, tralokinumab, risankizumab, secukinumab
- Dupilumab for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis routinely requires multi-step documentation of prior treatment failure across multiple insurers
- Biologics for dermatologic conditions frequently billed under medical benefit (Part B for Medicare Advantage)
- Published step therapy sequences inconsistently enforced: insurers approve requests bypassing stated requirements while denying others satisfying them
- Coverage criteria updated through internal guidance without published policy updates
- GreenLight PA platform: EHR-independent, no PHI by architectural design, enables deployment across all practice sizes

**8. IMPACT ASSESSMENT**

Affected Stakeholders:
- Dermatology practices (particularly independent practices)
- Patients awaiting access to dermatology biologics and specialty medications
- Specialty practices (dermatology, rheumatology, oncology)
- Healthcare providers prescribing biologics
- Payers (Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, commercial QHP issuers)
- Health IT developers building PA tools
- EHR vendors
- Specialty societies
- Researchers studying PA burden

Economic Implications:
- Reduced avoidable denials and resubmission cycles
- Decreased administrative burden from manual PDF policy interpretation
- Lower discovery burden for health IT developers
- Efficiency gains from EHR-independent middleware tools
- Cost of implementing mandatory CRD/DTR requirements for payers
- Cost of specialty-level metrics reporting disaggregation
- Cost of publishing structured, machine-readable step therapy requirements

Technical Feasibility:
- Da Vinci CRD and DTR implementation guides represent right technical direction
- FHIR and NCPDP standards provide foundation
- EHR-independent tools feasible (GreenLight PA demonstrates model)
- API endpoint publication with version/conformance information technically achievable
- Structured, machine-readable PA criteria publishing feasible without disclosing proprietary adjudication logic
- Policy intelligence layer remains product/workflow challenge even with standardized APIs

Patient Care Impact:
- Improved access to dermatology biologics and specialty medications
- Reduced delays in therapy access from avoidable denials and resubmission cycles
- Better alignment between published criteria and actual approval behavior improves predictability
- Faster approval processes with accurate payer-specific requirements at point of care
- Reduced administrative delays affecting patient outcomes
- Enhanced transparency enabling informed provider/patient decisions

**9. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS**
- Overall position: Strongly Supportive with Critical Enhancement Recommendations
- Tone: Professional, Technical, Evidence-Based, Constructively Critical
- Priority level: High

**10. KEY QUOTES**

"We write to draw CMS's attention to a structural problem in the prior authorization ecosystem that the proposed rule's transparency provisions begin to address but do not fully reach: the divergence between payers' published prior authorization criteria and the criteria actually applied in approval and denial decisions." - Identifies core systemic problem

"We have observed systematic patterns in which published payer criteria do not reliably predict actual approval behavior." - Evidence from 200+ drug-insurer-state combinations

"Providers build PA submissions around published criteria that may not reflect what the insurer actually requires, leading to avoidable denials, resubmission cycles, and delays in patient access to therapy." - Describes measurable harm

"The ability to submit a PA request electronically does not, by itself, ensure that providers understand what the payer requires for approval. The underlying PA criteria — step therapy requirements, diagnostic thresholds, prior treatment history requirements, quantity limits, and documentation standards — remain largely inaccessible in structured, machine-readable form." - Identifies gap in proposed rule

**11. THEMES**
- Interoperability (primary focus: FHIR, NCPDP, Da Vinci CRD/DTR/PAS standards)
- Provider Burden (PA submission preparation, manual PDF interpretation, administrative complexity)
- Transparency/Accountability (published vs. applied criteria divergence, public metrics reporting)
- Technology Standards (mandatory CRD/DTR, API endpoints, machine-readable criteria)
- Specialty Care (dermatology biologics, specialty-level metrics, practice workflows)
- Patient Access (therapy delays, avoidable denials, resubmission cycles)
- Step Therapy (inconsistent enforcement, variation across payers/states, documentation requirements)
- Health IT Development (EHR-independent tools, middleware, developer ecosystem)
- Data Standardization (structured PA criteria, machine-readable formats)
- Criteria Consistency (published policy vs. actual adjudication, internal guidance opacity)
